newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan bourse watchdog tightens rules.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan bourse watchdog tightens rules.

text.p: Morocco's stock exchange watchdog has devised new rules to ensure more transparent trading of shares, which it believes will be helped by the gradual introduction of electronic trading.

"With the new electronic trading, the CDVM (watchdog's) role will be easier. It will put an end to speculation arising because traders did not disclose their orders straightaway," Mohamed Amrani, spokesman for the Conseil Deontologique des Valeurs Mobilieres (CDVM) said in an interview with Reuters.

The law regulating trade on the Casablanca stock exchange, where 47 companies are listed, was amended last year and included a clause enabling a moral code to be drawn up for everyone trading on the bourse.
The CDVM drew up the code laying out minimum rules for trading.
"This is meant to prevent insider dealing. There was no code of ethics before," Amrani added.
The exchange last week started the gradual introduction of electronic trading.
CDVM was set up in 1994 and showed its teeth the following year when it delisted 18 companies which had refused to publish their annual results as requested by the watchdog.
"There were very small companies, some of which had not been traded for three or four years because there were very few stocks available," he said.
According to Amrani, among reasons these firms did not trade was the fact that many had only one or two shareholders and for others, a lack of transparency discouraged people from selling.
"These were mainly dormant companies, the 18 firms had a capitalisation of only 365 million dirhams ($39 million at current exchange rates) in 1994," he added.
Publication of results was not compulsory until the law was amended at the end of 1996.
"There was no control body to check that the companies submitted to the law, that's why only a few made them (their results) public," Amrani added.
He said that in 1994, a total of 29 companies did not publish their results or were late in handing them. Last year 99 percent of them met the deadline.
Last Monday, the CDVM in a statement published in the Moroccan newspaper l'Opinion asked firms to publish their results in approved newspapers by the end of this month.
